html:
A famine in the People's Republic of China from 1959 to 1961, often called the deadliest in human history and one of the worst disasters made by people. Estimates of excess deaths range widely, from a few million to over 50 million; many scholars put the figure between about 15 and 45 million.

Its main cause was policy. In 1958 Mao Zedong launched the Great Leap Forward, a push to overtake Britain's industry within years. Peasants were pooled into huge people's communes, private plots and cooking were banned and meals were eaten in communal canteens. Millions were pulled off the land to make iron in backyard furnaces.

How it turned into famine:

  • Officials, afraid of being branded rightists, reported harvests far bigger than real ones.
  • The state took grain based on these false numbers, leaving villages without food, and kept exporting grain.
  • Untested farming methods, such as very close planting and deep ploughing, cut yields.
  • A campaign to kill sparrows let insect pests multiply, and bad weather hit some areas.

When Defence Minister Peng Dehuai criticised the policy at the Lushan meeting of 1959, Mao purged him, and the campaign went on. The worst hit provinces included Anhui, Sichuan and Henan. The government hid the famine for decades and still calls these the "three years of difficulty".

The leadership retreated in the early 1960s, and leaders such as Deng Xiaoping restored some private plots. The memory of the famine helped drive the later turn to family farming in the household responsibility system.
